title: Process Injection: Ptrace System Calls
summary: This sub-technique uses ptrace, the Unix system call that lets one process observe and control another, to run code inside a live process. The call is the foundation of ordinary debugging, so the capability is present on every Linux host by design. An injector attaches to a target, writes its payload into the target's address space, and then changes the target's saved processor registers so that the next instruction executed is the payload, with the register holding the next instruction pointer as the primary lever. The same effect can be reached by copying data directly into a chosen address, for example into the memory holding the next instruction, without touching registers at all, and the target can then be detached and left running. Permission restrictions are part of the picture and a useful triage filter: attaching usually requires the same user or sufficient privilege, and a process that is not a child of the injector or is more privileged may simply refuse. Evidence comes from the audit trail if system call auditing is enabled, from process relationships, and from the state of the memory maps of the target, where a region that is writable and executable and is backed by no file on disk is the strongest signal.

beginner.definition: Ptrace is a Linux system call, which is a request a program makes to the operating system kernel. It is the tool that debuggers use to watch and control another running program. This sub-technique is when an attacker uses that same control to run their own code inside a target process. It is part of the Process Injection parent technique, and its home is Linux rather than Windows.
beginner.whyItMatters: The same ability that makes debugging possible also makes silent code placement possible. Because debuggers are legitimate, blocking ptrace outright would break everyday development work. Detecting abuse means knowing which process attached to which, and why. Attach restrictions based on user and privilege limit the technique but do not remove it.
howItWorks: The attacker starts a process or uses an existing one that is allowed to trace another process.
They attach to the target, which stops it and gives the tracer control over its state.
They write their code into the target's memory, using the access the tracer has.
They change the saved register that points at the next instruction, so the target will run the new code.
They detach or resume the target, which continues as the payload until it returns to normal work.
They can also copy data straight into the memory holding the next instruction without touching registers.
beginner.example: Picture a library reading room with a rule that a tutor may sit beside a student and guide them. Someone uses that permission to sit down, quietly replace the page the student is reading and walk away. The student keeps reading, now following words they never chose. The rule was followed, because a tutor is allowed to sit there. Only the sign in sheet shows who sat down and when.
takeaways: The debugging facility on Linux can be used to place code in another process.
Attach restrictions reduce the risk but do not cover every case.
Writable and executable memory without a backing file is a key clue.

objectives: Explain what ptrace is and why a debugging tool is needed to control another process.
Describe how register redirection makes a target run attacker code on its next instruction.
Explain the privilege and parent process limits that restrict this technique.
Identify the audit and memory telemetry that reveals an unexpected trace attach.
Explain why blocking ptrace entirely is not a practical control on most systems.
